topics.title: [Dev] Would a price ceiling on groceries help?

history.note: Debate topic for development and automated tests only. Not reviewed, real course material.

background: [Dev example] Imagine a hypothetical country where the price of a staple grain has risen sharply, putting heavy pressure on low-income households.

In the supply and demand model, a price ceiling set below the equilibrium price raises quantity demanded and lowers quantity supplied, which can cause a shortage. Real outcomes can depend on market structure, supporting government policies, and how suppliers respond.
topics.policy_question: Is a price ceiling on a staple grain a good way to help low-income households?

perspectives.name: Ease the price burden first
perspectives.summary: The view that protecting households who can't afford food right now comes first
reasoning: When prices rise, households that spend a large share of income on food are hit hardest.
assumptions: Assumes supply does not drop much in the short run.

perspectives.name: Worried about supply and shortages
perspectives.summary: The view that a price ceiling may cut supply and make the grain harder to find
reasoning: In the model, a price ceiling below equilibrium creates excess demand (a shortage).
assumptions: Assumes suppliers respond to the price by producing and selling less.

perspectives.name: Use targeted support instead
perspectives.summary: The view that prices should be left alone and households in need should get direct support
reasoning: It keeps the price signal while focusing support on the people who need it.
assumptions: Assumes the government can accurately identify who should get support.

guiding_questions: Who gains and who loses from a price ceiling?
If a shortage happens, how will the grain end up being divided?
When comparing direct support with a price ceiling, which criteria (efficiency, equity, feasibility) matter most?
trade_offs: Immediate price relief vs. lower supply and possible shortages
The same benefit for everyone vs. support focused on households in need

topics.title: [Dev] Should we introduce a carbon tax?

history.note: Debate topic for development and automated tests only. Not reviewed, real course material.

background: [Dev example] A carbon tax is a policy that taxes the production and consumption of high-emission goods to reduce emissions.

In the model, the tax raises the price consumers pay, lowers the price producers receive, and reduces the quantity traded. Whether society as a whole gains depends on how large you assume the damage from emissions is and how the tax revenue is used.
topics.policy_question: If we introduce a carbon tax, how should we set the tax rate and use the revenue?

perspectives.name: Cut emissions with a price signal
perspectives.summary: The view that putting the cost of emissions into prices lets everyone cut where cutting is cheapest
reasoning: Putting external damage into prices can move the market quantity closer to the socially optimal quantity.
assumptions: Assumes the size of the external damage can be roughly estimated.

perspectives.name: Worried about a fair burden
perspectives.summary: The view that households spending a large share on energy could be hit hard
reasoning: The tax burden is split between consumers and producers, and some households may bear a large burden relative to income.
assumptions: Assumes the revenue is not returned to households.

perspectives.name: Offset it by returning the revenue
perspectives.summary: The view that returning revenue to households or cutting other taxes can ease the burden
reasoning: Each household's net burden depends on how the revenue is used.
assumptions: Assumes a rebate program can be designed and run.

guiding_questions: How does the conclusion change depending on the external damage (md) you assume?
Who bears more of the tax, consumers or producers? What decides that?
How could the revenue be used to reduce fairness concerns?
trade_offs: Lower emissions vs. higher prices and a smaller quantity traded
Efficient emission cuts vs. a fair burden across households
